## Stochastic modeling solutions

These solutions use the shared root environment and keep the checks close to
the model code.  Seeds make the example output reproducible, but they do not
turn stochastic results into universal constants.

### Continuous-time Markov chains and jump processes

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-ch04-ex1}

The two infectious stages use rate $2\gamma$.  Their sum is an Erlang
distribution with mean $2/(2\gamma)=1/\gamma$, matching the original
single-stage mean, but variance $2/(2\gamma)^2=1/(2\gamma^2)$, half the
single exponential variance.

```{julia}
using Catalyst
using JumpProcesses
using StableRNGs

N, β, c, γ = 1000, 0.05, 10.0, 0.25
κ = β * c / N
network = @reaction_network begin
    κ, S + I₁ --> 2I₁
    κ, S + I₂ --> I₁ + I₂
    2γ, I₁ --> I₂
    2γ, I₂ --> R
end

u₀ = [:S => 990, :I₁ => 10, :I₂ => 0, :R => 0]
problem = JumpProblem(
    network, u₀, (0.0, 40.0), [:κ => κ, :γ => γ];
    aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(20250711),
)
solution = solve(problem, SSAStepper(); saveat = 0.2)
states = Array(solution)
mass_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(states; dims = 1)) .- N))
nonnegative = minimum(states) >= 0
integer_valued = all(x -> isapprox(x, round(x)), states)
@assert mass_error == 0
@assert nonnegative && integer_valued
(; mass_error, nonnegative, integer_valued)
```

Both stages transmit, so the total force of infection is
$\kappa S(I_1+I_2)$ and new infections always enter $I_1$.  The rates
$2\gamma$ preserve the total mean infectious duration at $1/\gamma$.  Allowing
both stages to transmit at the same per-capita rate makes the mean
transmitting duration equal to that total duration and therefore preserves
$R_0=\beta c/\gamma=2$; if only $I_1$ transmitted, the mean transmitting
duration and $R_0$ would both be halved.  The conservation check is exact because
every reaction removes one individual from one compartment and adds one to
another.  Compared with one exponential infectious period, the two-stage
construction reduces unrealistically short and long durations while preserving
the mean.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-ch04-ex2}

For an immigration--death count $Z$, a `DiscreteProblem` and two
`ConstantRateJump`s are sufficient.  Arrivals occur at the constant rate
$\lambda$, so their propensity does not depend on $Z$; departures occur at
rate $\mu$ per individual present, so their propensity is $\mu Z$.  Both are
`ConstantRateJump`s because neither rate depends explicitly on time.

```{julia}
using JumpProcesses
using StableRNGs

function arrival!(integrator)
    integrator.u[1] += 1
end
function departure!(integrator)
    integrator.u[1] -= 1
end

λ, μ = 0.8, 0.1
toy = DiscreteProblem([5], (0.0, 20.0), nothing)
arrival_rate(u, p, t) = λ              # constant immigration
departure_rate(u, p, t) = μ * u[1]     # per-individual departure
arrival_jump = ConstantRateJump(arrival_rate, arrival!)
departure_jump = ConstantRateJump(departure_rate, departure!)
toy_problem = JumpProblem(
    toy, Direct(), arrival_jump, departure_jump;
    rng = StableRNG(20250712),
)
toy_solution = solve(toy_problem, SSAStepper())
@assert minimum(reduce(vcat, toy_solution.u)) >= 0
```

No boundary guard is needed in `departure!`: the propensity $\mu Z$ vanishes
at $Z=0$, so the departure jump cannot fire from the empty state and the count
cannot go negative.

To add vaccination to SIR, introduce the transition $S\to R$ with propensity
$a_{\mathrm{vac}}=\nu S$.  With $\nu$ constant, all three propensities depend
only on the state and are constant between events, so each is a
`ConstantRateJump` and the direct method applies unchanged:

```{julia}
function infection!(integrator)
    integrator.u[1] -= 1
    integrator.u[2] += 1
end
function recovery!(integrator)
    integrator.u[2] -= 1
    integrator.u[3] += 1
end
function vaccinate!(integrator)
    integrator.u[1] -= 1
    integrator.u[3] += 1
end

ν = 0.01
sir = DiscreteProblem([990, 10, 0], (0.0, 40.0), nothing)
infection_jump = ConstantRateJump(
    (u, p, t) -> κ * u[1] * u[2], infection!
)
recovery_jump = ConstantRateJump(
    (u, p, t) -> γ * u[2], recovery!
)
vaccination_jump = ConstantRateJump(
    (u, p, t) -> ν * u[1], vaccinate!
)

vaccinated_problem = JumpProblem(
    sir, Direct(),
    infection_jump, recovery_jump, vaccination_jump;
    rng = StableRNG(20250713),
)
vaccinated_solution = solve(vaccinated_problem, SSAStepper(); saveat = 0.2)
vaccinated_states = Array(vaccinated_solution)
@assert maximum(abs.(vec(sum(vaccinated_states; dims = 1)) .- 1000)) == 0
@assert minimum(vaccinated_states) >= 0
```

The mean-field equations become
$$
\dot S=-\kappa SI-\nu S,\quad
\dot I=\kappa SI-\gamma I,\quad
\dot R=\gamma I+\nu S.
$$

Updating the ODE comparison means carrying the same $-\nu S$ and $+\nu S$
terms in the drift, then reading the two side by side:

```{julia}
using OrdinaryDiffEq

function vaccination_drift!(du, u, p, t)
    κ, γ, ν = p
    infection = κ * u[1] * u[2]
    du[1] = -infection - ν * u[1]
    du[2] = infection - γ * u[2]
    du[3] = γ * u[2] + ν * u[1]
    return nothing
end

vaccinated_ode = solve(
    ODEProblem(vaccination_drift!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, 40.0), (κ, γ, ν)),
    Tsit5(); saveat = 0.2,
)
vaccinated_ode_states = Array(vaccinated_ode)
(; jump_peak_I = maximum(vaccinated_states[2, :]),
   ode_peak_I = round(maximum(vaccinated_ode_states[2, :]); digits = 1),
   jump_final_R = vaccinated_states[3, end],
   ode_final_R = round(vaccinated_ode_states[3, end]; digits = 1))
```

One stochastic path is not expected to match the mean-field curve; the
comparison is a sanity check that adding the same term to both descriptions
moves them in the same direction, not a precision test.

If $\nu=\nu(t)$, vaccination is a `VariableRateJump`.  With a known upper
bound for $\nu(t)$ over each interval, it can be encoded as a bounded
`VariableRateJump` and simulated using `Coevolve()` with `SSAStepper()`; the
supplied `urate` and `rateinterval` must bound $\nu(s)S$ throughout
that interval.  Without convenient bounds, use a general `VariableRateJump`
with a continuous base problem and solver.  A piecewise-constant campaign can
instead be handled in successive intervals or with scheduled parameter
changes; a callback that changes parameters mid-simulation must then call
`reset_aggregated_jumps!(integrator)`, because the aggregator caches the
current propensities and the time of the next event and would otherwise keep
using the pre-change values until the next jump fires.

### Stochastic differential equations

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-ch05-ex1}

The experiment keeps the model, seed, and output grid fixed while changing the
Euler--Maruyama step.  Conservation is a structural property of the
reaction-level noise, whereas nonnegativity is not guaranteed by any finite
`dt`.

```{julia}
using StochasticDiffEq
using StableRNGs

N, β, c, γ = 1000.0, 0.05, 10.0, 0.25
κ = β * c / N
u₀ = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]

function f!(du, u, p, t)
    κ, γ = p
    a₁ = κ * max(u[1], 0.0) * max(u[2], 0.0)
    a₂ = γ * max(u[2], 0.0)
    du[1], du[2], du[3] = -a₁, a₁ - a₂, a₂
end
function g!(G, u, p, t)
    κ, γ = p
    a₁ = κ * max(u[1], 0.0) * max(u[2], 0.0)
    a₂ = γ * max(u[2], 0.0)
    s₁, s₂ = sqrt(a₁), sqrt(a₂)
    G[1, 1], G[2, 1], G[3, 1] = -s₁, s₁, 0.0
    G[1, 2], G[2, 2], G[3, 2] = 0.0, -s₂, s₂
end

function run_sde(dt)
    problem = SDEProblem(
        f!, g!, u₀, (0.0, 30.0), (κ, γ);
        noise_rate_prototype = zeros(3, 2),
    )
    solution = solve(
        problem, LambaEM();
        dt, adaptive = false, saveat = 0.1,
        rng = StableRNG(20250711),
    )
    states = Array(solution)
    (
        dt = dt,
        conservation_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(states; dims = 1)) .- N)),
        minimum_state = minimum(states),
    )
end

results = run_sde.( (0.1, 0.05, 0.01) )
@assert all(result.conservation_error < 1e-8 for result in results)
results
```

The conservation error stays at roundoff level for every step size, and this
is not a statement about accuracy: each column of $G$ sums to zero, so both
the drift and every Euler increment lie in the population-conserving subspace
whatever `dt` is.  Nonnegativity has no such structural protection.  From a
fixed state strictly inside the nonnegative region, reducing `dt` generally
reduces the probability and the size of a one-step discretization overshoot.
It does not make the diffusion nonnegative.  This model starts at $R=0$ while
the recovery diffusion coefficient is already nonzero, so negative $R$ values
remain possible as `dt` is refined — and their first-step probability need not
decrease.  Writing $a_2=\gamma I$ for the recovery propensity at $t=0$, the
first Euler--Maruyama step gives
$$
R_{\Delta t}=a_2\Delta t+\sqrt{a_2\Delta t}\,Z,\qquad Z\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,1),
$$

so $P(R_{\Delta t}<0)=\Phi(-\sqrt{a_2\Delta t})$, which *increases* towards
$1/2$ as $\Delta t\to0$.  With $a_2=\gamma I(0)=2.5$ that probability is about
$0.31$ at $\Delta t=0.1$, $0.36$ at $0.05$, and $0.44$ at $0.01$.  Refinement
removes discretization overshoot from the interior; it cannot remove boundary
crossings intrinsic to the Gaussian diffusion.  If nonnegativity is essential,
use the integer CTMC or a principled boundary-preserving method rather than
silently clipping the output.

The three runs share a seed but not a Wiener path.  Each solve draws its
random numbers on its own time grid, so the differences in `minimum_state`
above mix discretization effects with different Brownian realizations and are
not a pathwise convergence measurement.  To measure strong convergence,
generate the noise once and reuse it across the solves with `NoiseWrapper`
from `DiffEqNoiseProcess`.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-ch05-ex2}

Independent state noise has a diagonal $3\times3$ diffusion.  The comparison
below uses the same drift and seed as the reaction-level SDE.  The shared seed
makes both runs reproducible; it does not give them a common Wiener path,
because the two models have different noise dimensions and different diffusion
matrices — two Wiener processes against three.  The trajectory comparison is
therefore illustrative rather than pathwise.

```{julia}
using StochasticDiffEq
using StableRNGs

function diagonal_g!(G, u, p, t)
    κ, γ = p
    a₁ = κ * max(u[1], 0.0) * max(u[2], 0.0)
    a₂ = γ * max(u[2], 0.0)
    fill!(G, 0.0)
    G[1, 1] = sqrt(a₁)
    G[2, 2] = sqrt(a₁ + a₂)
    G[3, 3] = sqrt(a₂)
end

reaction_problem = SDEProblem(
    f!, g!, u₀, (0.0, 30.0), (κ, γ);
    noise_rate_prototype = zeros(3, 2),
)
diagonal_problem = SDEProblem(
    f!, diagonal_g!, u₀, (0.0, 30.0), (κ, γ);
    noise_rate_prototype = zeros(3, 3),
)
reaction_solution = solve(
    reaction_problem, LambaEM();
    dt = 0.02, adaptive = false, saveat = 0.1,
    rng = StableRNG(20250711),
)
diagonal_solution = solve(
    diagonal_problem, LambaEM();
    dt = 0.02, adaptive = false, saveat = 0.1,
    rng = StableRNG(20250711),
)
reaction_states, diagonal_states = Array(reaction_solution), Array(diagonal_solution)
reaction_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(reaction_states; dims = 1)) .- 1000))
diagonal_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(diagonal_states; dims = 1)) .- 1000))
(; reaction_error, diagonal_error,
    infected_difference = maximum(abs.(reaction_states[2, :] .- diagonal_states[2, :])))
```

For the reaction model $Q=GG^\mathsf{T}$ has
$$
Q_{12}=Q_{21}=-a_1,\qquad Q_{23}=Q_{32}=-a_2,\qquad Q_{13}=0.
$$

The two terms lost are therefore $\operatorname{Cov}(dS,dI)=-a_1\,dt$ and
$\operatorname{Cov}(dI,dR)=-a_2\,dt$: an infection moves one person out of $S$
and into $I$, and a recovery moves one out of $I$ and into $R$, so those pairs
of increments are perfectly anticorrelated at the reaction level.  The
diagonal model sets both to zero while keeping the marginal variances
$a_1$, $a_1+a_2$, and $a_2$.  Summing the diagonal increments then gives
$$
\operatorname{Var}(dS+dI+dR)=\bigl(a_1+(a_1+a_2)+a_2\bigr)dt=2(a_1+a_2)\,dt,
$$

instead of the zero the reaction-level model gives, which is exactly why the
total population no longer stays at $N$.  Its conservation error is therefore
not a roundoff diagnostic, and its infected trajectory is a different
stochastic model, not merely a noisier numerical solve.

The two conservation errors are directly comparable, because conservation is
structural and holds path by path.  The reported `infected_difference` is not:
with no common Wiener path behind the two solves, it measures one arbitrary
pair of realizations rather than the discrepancy between the models.  To
quantify that discrepancy, run ensembles of both and compare the mean,
standard deviation, or full distribution of the peak $I$, as the chapter does
for the jump process and the reaction-level SDE.

### Reaction networks and moment closure

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-ch06-ex1}

Adding a latent class is an edit to the network, not a rewrite of the dynamics:
the two lowerings follow from the amended specification exactly as before.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-ch06-ex1
using Catalyst
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using JumpProcesses
using CairoMakie
using StableRNGs
using Statistics

const N_seir = 1000
const κ_seir = 0.05 * 10.0 / N_seir
const γ_seir = 0.25
const σ_seir = 0.5
const seir_tspan = (0.0, 60.0)
const seir_times = collect(0.0:0.5:60.0)

seir_network = @reaction_network begin
    κ, S + I --> E + I
    σ, E --> I
    γ, I --> R
end

seir_parameters = [:κ => κ_seir, :σ => σ_seir, :γ => γ_seir]
seir_ode = solve(
    ODEProblem(seir_network, [:S => 990.0, :E => 0.0, :I => 10.0, :R => 0.0],
               seir_tspan, seir_parameters),
    Tsit5(); saveat = seir_times)

function simulate_seir(seed)
    problem = JumpProblem(
        seir_network, [:S => 990, :E => 0, :I => 10, :R => 0],
        seir_tspan, seir_parameters;
        aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(seed))
    return Array(solve(problem, SSAStepper(); saveat = seir_times)(seir_times))
end

seir_ensemble = cat((simulate_seir(7000 + k) for k in 1:100)...; dims = 3)
seir_mean = dropdims(mean(seir_ensemble; dims = 3), dims = 3)
infectious_row = findfirst(==("I(t)"), string.(species(seir_network)))
(ode_peak_time = seir_times[argmax(seir_ode[infectious_row, :])],
 ensemble_peak_time = seir_times[argmax(seir_mean[infectious_row, :])])
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-sol-ch06-ex1
#| fig-cap: "SEIR infectious class: the ODE lowering (dashed) against the mean of 100 jump trajectories (solid), both generated from one reaction network."
figure = Figure(size = (720, 340))
axis = Axis(figure[1, 1], xlabel = "Time", ylabel = "Infectious")
lines!(axis, seir_times, seir_mean[infectious_row, :]; color = :grey25,
       linewidth = 2, label = "Jump ensemble mean")
lines!(axis, seir_times, seir_ode[infectious_row, :]; color = :steelblue,
       linewidth = 2, linestyle = :dash, label = "ODE")
axislegend(axis; position = :rt, framevisible = false)
figure
```

The latent class delays and flattens the peak relative to the SIR model of
@sec-reaction-networks. An infected individual now waits in $E$ for a mean
$1/\sigma = 2$ days before becoming infectious, so the generation interval
lengthens and the same $R_0$ is realised more slowly. The gap between the ODE
and the ensemble mean persists for the reason given in @eq-ch06-unclosed: the
transmission propensity is still bimolecular, so the ODE still discards
$\operatorname{Cov}(S,I)$.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-ch06-ex2}

Shrinking the population while holding the per-contact rates fixed makes the
relative fluctuations larger, which is precisely where a normal closure is
expected to struggle.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-ch06-ex2
#| warning: false
using MomentClosure

function closure_versus_ensemble(population; trajectories = 200, seed0 = 8000)
    κ_local = 0.05 * 10.0 / population
    network = @reaction_network begin
        κ, S + I --> 2I
        γ, I --> R
    end
    parameters_local = [:κ => κ_local, :γ => 0.25]
    S₀ = 0.99 * population
    I₀ = 0.01 * population
    span = (0.0, 40.0)
    grid = collect(0.0:0.5:40.0)

    raw = generate_raw_moment_eqs(network, 2)
    closed = moment_closure(raw, "normal")
    closure = solve(ODEProblem(closed, [S₀, I₀, 0.0], span, parameters_local),
                    Tsit5(); saveat = grid)
    names = string.(unknowns(closed.odes))
    mean_series = closure[findfirst(==("μ₀₁₀(t)"), names), :]

    function one_run(seed)
        problem = JumpProblem(
            network, [:S => round(Int, S₀), :I => round(Int, I₀), :R => 0],
            span, parameters_local; aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(seed))
        return Array(solve(problem, SSAStepper(); saveat = grid)(grid))
    end
    ensemble = cat((one_run(seed0 + k) for k in 1:trajectories)...; dims = 3)
    ensemble_mean = dropdims(mean(ensemble; dims = 3), dims = 3)[2, :]

    # At small N the closure can terminate early, returning fewer saved points
    # than requested, so compare only over the range it actually produced.
    n = min(length(mean_series), length(ensemble_mean))
    gap = maximum(abs.(mean_series[1:n] .- ensemble_mean[1:n]))
    return (population = population,
            closure_retcode = closure.retcode,
            points_returned = n,
            max_absolute_gap = round(gap; digits = 3),
            relative_to_population = round(gap / population; digits = 4))
end

[closure_versus_ensemble(1000), closure_versus_ensemble(100)]
```

The result at $N=100$ is sharper than a larger error: the solver returns
`ReturnCode.Unstable` and stops early, so only part of the time range is
comparable at all. The normal closure does not gracefully degrade here — it
breaks.

The argument after @eq-ch06-unclosed explains why. The closure is exact except
for the neglected third central moments, and their size relative to the first two
scales roughly as $N^{-1/2}$: with fewer individuals the distribution of $I$ is
further from normal and more skewed. Worse, a noticeable fraction of runs go
extinct before an outbreak takes off, so the true distribution has an atom of
probability at zero. A symmetric closure has no way to represent that, and the
variance it infers can go negative — at which point the moment equations lose any
solution to follow and the integration fails.

This is the practical lesson of the chapter's limitations section in concrete
form: always check the return code before reading the numbers.

### Agent-based models

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-ch07-ex1}

The grid model changes the contact assumption: a susceptible samples only
agents in its Moore neighborhood.  `GridSpaceSingle` holds at most one agent
per cell, so filling every cell of a periodic $40\times25$ grid gives the same
$N=1000$ population as the chapter, with exactly eight neighbors each and no
boundary special cases.  `GridAgent{2}` supplies `pos`, and `:chebyshev` is
the metric under which radius 1 is the Moore neighborhood.  The radius is a
model property here only so the same code can answer the final part of the
question.

```{julia}
using Agents
using Distributions
using Random
using Statistics
using StableRNGs

@agent struct GridPerson(GridAgent{2})
    status::Symbol
    next_status::Symbol
end

function grid_agent_step!(person, model)
    person.next_status = person.status
    if person.status == :S
        neighbors = collect(nearby_agents(person, model, model.radius))
        for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt))
            contact = rand(abmrng(model), neighbors)
            if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < model.β
                person.next_status = :I
                break
            end
        end
    elseif person.status == :I &&
           rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt)
        person.next_status = :R
    end
end

function grid_model_step!(model)
    for person in allagents(model)
        person.status = person.next_status
    end
end

grid_S(model) = count(p.status == :S for p in allagents(model))
grid_I(model) = count(p.status == :I for p in allagents(model))
grid_R(model) = count(p.status == :R for p in allagents(model))

function run_grid(seed, radius; max_steps = 2000)
    space = GridSpaceSingle((40, 25); periodic = true, metric = :chebyshev)
    model = StandardABM(
        GridPerson, space;
        agent_step! = grid_agent_step!,
        model_step! = grid_model_step!,
        properties = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, Δt = 0.1, radius = radius),
        rng = StableRNG(seed),
    )
    for position in positions(model)
        add_agent!(position, model; status = :S, next_status = :S)
    end
    for id in shuffle(abmrng(model), collect(allids(model)))[1:10]
        model[id].status = :I
        model[id].next_status = :I
    end
    S_history = Int[grid_S(model)]
    I_history = Int[grid_I(model)]
    R_history = Int[grid_R(model)]
    for _ in 1:max_steps
        grid_I(model) == 0 && break
        step!(model, 1)
        push!(S_history, grid_S(model))
        push!(I_history, grid_I(model))
        push!(R_history, grid_R(model))
    end
    @assert grid_I(model) == 0 "increase max_steps: epidemic has not ended"
    return hcat(S_history, I_history, R_history)'
end

counts = run_grid(20250714, 1)
@assert maximum(abs.(vec(sum(counts; dims = 1)) .- 1000)) == 0
@assert counts[:, 1] == [990, 10, 0]
@assert all(diff(counts[1, :]) .<= 0)

grid_summary = map((1, 5)) do radius
    runs = [run_grid(6000 + k, radius) for k in 1:8]
    final_sizes = [path[3, end] for path in runs]
    (; radius, neighbors = (2radius + 1)^2 - 1,
       mean_final_size = mean(final_sizes), sd = round(std(final_sizes); digits = 1))
end
```

The well-mixed model of the chapter, run to the same extinction criterion and
with the same eight seeds, is the reference the grid results are compared
against.

```{julia}
@agent struct MixedPerson(NoSpaceAgent)
    status::Symbol
    next_status::Symbol
end

function mixed_agent_step!(person, model)
    person.next_status = person.status
    if person.status == :S
        for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt))
            contact = random_agent(model)
            if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < model.β
                person.next_status = :I
                break
            end
        end
    elseif person.status == :I &&
           rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt)
        person.next_status = :R
    end
end

function run_mixed(seed; max_steps = 2000)
    model = StandardABM(
        MixedPerson;
        agent_step! = mixed_agent_step!,
        model_step! = grid_model_step!,
        properties = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, Δt = 0.1),
        rng = StableRNG(seed),
    )
    for id in 1:1000
        status = id <= 10 ? :I : :S
        add_agent!(MixedPerson(; id, status, next_status = status), model)
    end
    for _ in 1:max_steps
        grid_I(model) == 0 && break
        step!(model, 1)
    end
    @assert grid_I(model) == 0 "increase max_steps: epidemic has not ended"
    return grid_R(model)
end

mixed_final_sizes = [run_mixed(6000 + k) for k in 1:8]
well_mixed_reference = (;
    mean_final_size = mean(mixed_final_sizes),
    sd = round(std(mixed_final_sizes); digits = 1),
)
```

```{julia}
(; grid = grid_summary, well_mixed = well_mixed_reference)
```

Conservation still holds, because the update changes a status but never
creates or removes an agent.  The epidemic, however, usually stays localized
and much smaller: with the eight-cell neighborhood the mean final size over
eight seeds is a small fraction of the well-mixed reference printed above,
and the spread across seeds is enormous: a standard deviation above 100,
with some seeds fizzling after a few dozen infections and others reaching a
couple of hundred.  This is not a small correction to mass action but a
qualitatively different regime.

The well-mixed reference itself should be compared against the exact ODE final
size, which solves $s_\infty=s_0e^{-R_0(1-s_\infty)}$ with $s_0=0.99$ rather
than the $1-x=e^{-R_0x}$ form, the latter being the negligible-initial-
infection approximation:

```{julia}
function ode_final_size(s₀, R₀)
    s = 0.5
    for _ in 1:500
        s = s₀ * exp(-R₀ * (1 - s))
    end
    return round(1000 * (1 - s); digits = 1)
end

(; exact = ode_final_size(0.99, 2.0), negligible_i₀ = ode_final_size(1.0, 2.0))
```

The assumption that fails is the one behind
$\Pr(\text{contact is infectious})=I_t/N$ in Equation @eq-abm-infection:
that a contact is a uniform draw from the whole population, so that the
*global* prevalence is the right infection risk.  On the grid a susceptible
draws from eight fixed neighbors, so what matters is the *local* prevalence,
and the two decouple.  Neighborhoods overlap heavily (an infective's
neighbors are largely each other's neighbors), so an agent's contacts are
rapidly used up on people its infector has already reached.

It is worth being precise about what has and has not stayed fixed.  The
parameter combination $\beta c/\gamma=2$ is unchanged, but that number is the
*mass-action* reproduction number; it is not the spatial model's $R_0$.  With
a finite neighborhood of degree $d$, repeated contacts land on the same few
people, so the number of *distinct* susceptibles an index case reaches is
smaller.  Writing $p=1-e^{-c\Delta t\beta/d}$ for the per-step probability of
transmitting to one particular neighbor and $q=1-e^{-\gamma\Delta t}$ for the
per-step recovery probability, the chance that a given neighbor is infected
before the focal agent recovers is $T=p/(p+q-pq)$:

```{julia}
function transmissibility(d; c = 10.0, β = 0.05, γ = 0.25, Δt = 0.1)
    p = 1 - exp(-c * Δt * β / d)
    q = 1 - exp(-γ * Δt)
    T = p / (p + q - p * q)
    return (; d, T = round(T; digits = 4),
              index_case = round(d * T; digits = 3),
              later_case = round((d - 1) * T; digits = 3))
end

transmissibility.((8, 120))
```

An isolated index case at radius 1 therefore makes about 1.62 distinct
infections rather than 2, and every later case draws from a neighborhood
already reached by its own infector, leaving at most $(d-1)T\approx1.42$ even
before the heavy clustering of the Moore lattice is taken into account.  That
margin above 1 is thin enough that local depletion and correlation can push
the effective reproduction number to or below 1, which is why so many seeds
fizzle.

Widening the neighborhood is the direct test of that explanation: at radius 5
each agent has 120 neighbors.  The pool is still fixed (it never refreshes),
but it is large enough that repeated-contact depletion and local correlation
become weak, $dT$ rises to about 1.99, and the mean final size returns to the
well-mixed value within the seed-to-seed scatter of both.  Mass action is
recovered in the limit of a large neighborhood, which is exactly the limit in
which "uniform over the population" becomes a fair description of local
mixing.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-ch07-ex2}

The physical horizon is held at 30 time units, so each run uses
`round(Int, 30 / Δt)` updates.  Each timestep gets its own seeded ensemble,
and each ensemble is reduced twice: once by averaging the trajectories and
then taking a maximum, and once by taking each trajectory's maximum and then
averaging.  400 replicates keep the standard error near 1 person, well below
the differences being compared.

```{julia}
@agent struct Person(NoSpaceAgent)
    status::Symbol
    next_status::Symbol
end

function agent_step!(person, model)
    person.next_status = person.status
    if person.status == :S
        for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt))
            contact = random_agent(model)
            if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < model.β
                person.next_status = :I
                break
            end
        end
    elseif person.status == :I &&
           rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt)
        person.next_status = :R
    end
end

function model_step!(model)
    for person in allagents(model)
        person.status = person.next_status
    end
end

infected_count(model) = count(p.status == :I for p in allagents(model))

function infectious_path(seed, Δt, nsteps)
    model = StandardABM(
        Person;
        agent_step!,
        model_step!,
        properties = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, Δt = Δt),
        rng = StableRNG(seed),
    )
    for id in 1:1000
        status = id <= 10 ? :I : :S
        add_agent!(Person(; id, status, next_status = status), model)
    end
    _, data = run!(
        model, nsteps;
        mdata = [infected_count],
        showprogress = false,
    )
    return collect(data.infected_count)
end

nreplicates = 400
nbootstrap = 400
fadeout_threshold = 50
peak_summary = map((0.2, 0.1, 0.05)) do Δt
    paths = [
        infectious_path(9000 + replicate, Δt, round(Int, 30 / Δt))
        for replicate in 1:nreplicates
    ]
    trajectories = reduce(hcat, paths)
    pathwise_peaks = maximum.(paths)
    mean_path = vec(mean(trajectories; dims = 2))
    boot_rng = StableRNG(4242)
    bootstrap_peaks = [
        maximum(vec(mean(
            trajectories[:, rand(boot_rng, 1:nreplicates, nreplicates)]; dims = 2,
        )))
        for _ in 1:nbootstrap
    ]
    (; Δt,
       peak_of_mean = round(maximum(mean_path); digits = 1),
       se_peak_of_mean = round(std(bootstrap_peaks); digits = 2),
       mean_of_peaks = round(mean(pathwise_peaks); digits = 1),
       sd_of_peaks = round(std(pathwise_peaks); digits = 1),
       se_mean_of_peaks = round(std(pathwise_peaks) / sqrt(nreplicates); digits = 2),
       fadeouts = count(peak -> peak < fadeout_threshold, pathwise_peaks),
       mean_excluding_fadeouts = round(
           mean(filter(>=(fadeout_threshold), pathwise_peaks)); digits = 1,
       ))
end
```

The two standard errors are computed differently on purpose.  The per-replicate
peaks are independent draws, so `se_mean_of_peaks` is the ordinary
$\mathrm{sd}/\sqrt{n}$.  `peak_of_mean` is a maximum taken *after* averaging,
which has no closed-form standard error, so it is bootstrapped by resampling
whole trajectories with replacement and recomputing the statistic each time.

```{julia}
peak_summary
```

The two columns are different statistics, and the ODE peak of $158.5$ falls
between them at every timestep.  `mean_of_peaks` estimates
$\mathbb{E}[\max_t I(t)]$ and sits above; `peak_of_mean` estimates
$\max_t\mathbb{E}[I(t)]$ and sits below.  The ordering is not an accident:
the maximum is a convex function, so Jensen's inequality forces
$\max_t\mathbb{E}[I(t)]\le\mathbb{E}[\max_t I(t)]$ for any ensemble.

Peak-time variation is the dominant reason the ensemble-mean curve is
flattened.  Here a fadeout is defined operationally as a run that never
reaches 50 simultaneous infectives.  Such runs are rare but not absent: the
`fadeouts` column counts a handful out of 400, and they are genuine early
extinctions in which the epidemic never grew beyond its 10 seed infectives.
That rate is the expected order of magnitude: treating the seeds as
independent branching processes, all ten die out with probability
$R_0^{-10}\approx0.1\%$.  The remaining runs take off at different moments,
and individual peaks land anywhere from about $t=12$ to $t=30$.  Averaging at
fixed clock time therefore adds up curves that are not aligned, and the
resulting mean is flatter and lower than any of them.  Aligning the paths on
their own peaks before averaging recovers `mean_of_peaks` exactly.

The fadeouts are far too few to account for the gap: `mean_excluding_fadeouts`
differs from `mean_of_peaks` by at most about one person, so removing them
would leave the picture unchanged.  Ruling out an extinction mixture
is not, however, the same as ruling out every stochastic effect.  Demographic
noise, variation in path height as well as timing, and the fact that
$\mathbb{E}[SI]\neq\mathbb{E}[S]\mathbb{E}[I]$ all contribute to the
difference between the ensemble and any deterministic curve.

Only part of the movement down the table is a timestep effect, and the two
parts can be separated by removing the randomness.  The deterministic
mean-field map that the ABM approximates for large $N$ applies exactly the
same frozen-within-a-step update rule, so its distance from the ODE is pure
discretization error.

```{julia}
function mean_field_peak(Δt)
    S, I = 990.0, 10.0
    peak = I
    for _ in 1:round(Int, 30 / Δt)
        new_infections = S * (1 - exp(-10.0 * 0.05 * Δt * I / 1000))
        new_recoveries = I * (1 - exp(-0.25 * Δt))
        S -= new_infections
        I += new_infections - new_recoveries
        peak = max(peak, I)
    end
    return round(peak; digits = 1)
end

[(; Δt, map_peak = mean_field_peak(Δt)) for Δt in (0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.01)]
```

The map's peak approaches the ODE's $158.5$ from above and roughly halves its
error each time $\Delta t$ halves: that is the timestep component, and it is
worth only a few people at $\Delta t=0.1$.  The update freezes the state over
each interval: agents infected during a step cannot recover or transmit until
the next one, while agents selected to recover remain infectious for the
whole current step.  These approximations act in opposing directions; for
these parameters their net effect biases the map's peak upward.

Everything else in the table is stochastic and will not go away.  Measuring
the two ensemble statistics against the map at the same $\Delta t$ separates
the pieces:

```{julia}
[(; s.Δt,
   map_peak = mean_field_peak(s.Δt),
   smearing = round(s.mean_of_peaks - s.peak_of_mean; digits = 1),
   max_inflation = round(s.mean_of_peaks - mean_field_peak(s.Δt); digits = 1),
   net_deficit = round(s.peak_of_mean - mean_field_peak(s.Δt); digits = 1))
 for s in peak_summary]
```

The net deficit of `peak_of_mean` against the map is twelve to thirteen
people, but it is not a single effect: it is twenty to twenty-three people of
temporal smearing, partly offset by seven to ten people of upward inflation in
the pathwise maximum.  Quoting the net figure alone would hide both of the
larger quantities that produce it.  None of the three shrinks systematically as
$\Delta t$ falls, which is the point: neither statistic converges to $158.5$,
and refining $\Delta t$ moves `peak_of_mean` further below the ODE peak rather
than towards it.  Reading the whole difference from $158.5$ as numerical error
would therefore be a mistake.

Changing $\Delta t$ also changes the model, not only its accuracy: the contact
and recovery probabilities are re-derived for a different interval, so this is
not purely a solver-error study.  `peak_of_mean` is the closest like-for-like
comparison with the ODE trajectory, since the ODE state is a population mean,
but at fixed finite $N$ it is not expected to equal the ODE peak.  Agreement
should only be expected in the joint limit of small $\Delta t$ and large $N$,
where finite-population stochastic effects, including peak-time scatter,
become negligible.
